name: Hassan Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick in the chilled section of a big grocery distribution centre, the one that supplies about sixty supermarkets. Shift starts at six, I put on the thermal jacket, grab a pallet truck and the scanner tells me where to go: yoghurts, cheese, ready meals, all stacked onto roll cages for the stores. I've been there six years, so I know the aisles without looking. The cold gets into your knuckles by ten, but the pay's good because of the chilled allowance and the union deal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew. Kofi and I have eaten lunch at the same table in the canteen for five years, and we talk football and politics and argue about both. What wears me out is the rate, the number on the scanner telling you you're at 94 percent when you've been running all morning. And my right knee, which clicks on the stairs now, and I'm only twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at union meetings: the tech was never the problem, it's who controls it. If AI just shaves a bit of time off the paperwork in the office, fine, nobody on the floor loses sleep. Online I'd probably share something about how the billionaires oversold it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays as it is, and that's mostly good. I've got over a year's pay saved, Giulia's a nurse, we're fine. The real fight is still the rate on the scanner and the cold, not some chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep going to the health-and-safety committee, because that's where the actual changes get made. I'd push again for longer warm-up breaks in chilled, which we've been asking for since last winter. And I'd keep putting the same 400 a month into savings, nothing special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest, because I've been telling Kofi for years it was hype. But the cold and the knee don't go away just because the robots didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mention the knee. How long do you see yourself doing this work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe another eight or ten years if the knee holds. My dad did warehouse work until fifty and he walks like a shopping trolley with a bad wheel now. I don't want that, but I also don't want to sit at a desk all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes with AI, what would you still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company getting bought. There were rumours last spring that a bigger chain wanted the site. A new owner could tear up our union deal in a week, and that worries me more than any AI story.

say: The **technology** was never the problem; what matters is **who controls it**.
If AI only speeds up **office paperwork**, nobody on the warehouse floor needs to lose sleep over it.
think: My life stays the same, and with **a year's pay saved** and my partner nursing, that feels fine.
The real fights are still the **pick rate** and the **cold** in the chilled section.
do: Keep working his six o'clock shifts and going to the **safety committee**.
Push again for **longer warm-up breaks** in the chilled section this winter.
Keep putting **400 a month** into savings, with no change to the plan.
feel: **Relieved** and a little smug, because he always said AI was overhyped.
Still **worn down** by the cold and his clicking right knee.
S0.quote: My dad did warehouse work until fifty and he walks like a shopping trolley with a bad wheel now.
fieldNote: His identity runs through the **union**; every question turns back to who controls the work.
The bigger worry is a **takeover** tearing up the union deal, not AI.
Strong savings and a nursing partner make this world feel **secure** to him, apart from his body.

steps.text: Keep working chilled-section shifts and attending the safety committee
Push the union for longer warm-up breaks in chilled this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing louder: if the office gets AI and the floor gets robots, the union needs to be at the table before the contract's signed, not after. I'd post the article in the union group chat and tag the rep. People would roll their eyes, but somebody has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office lot get hit first and we get a few years. The planners who build our pick routes, the woman who books the lorries, they're the ones I'd worry about now. But the robots come for us eventually, and I'd rather not be the last one standing in the aisle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to negotiate a no-redundancy clause tied to any new robots, with retraining paid by the company. I'd keep my savings where they are and stop thinking about a bigger flat for now. I wouldn't touch any AI tools myself, I'm not interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a rumour on the night shift and nobody will say if it's true. I'd keep going, but it'd sit in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Precious in transport planning books every lorry out of the yard. If software does the booking, Precious is out before I am, and Precious has two kids. I haven't got any, so I'd worry about her first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch AI tools. Is that a choice you'd stick with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, for now. I've never used one and I don't trust what they do with your data. If the union ran a course I might go, but I'm not going home to play with a chatbot after ten hours in the cold.

say: The union must be **at the table** before any robot contract is signed, not after.
He'd share the news in the **union group chat** and tag the rep, even if people roll their eyes.
think: The **office staff** get hit first; floor workers like him probably get a **few years**.
The robots come for **pickers** in the end, and he doesn't want to be the last one left.
do: Ask the union to bargain a **no-redundancy clause** tied to any new robots.
Push for **company-paid retraining** written into the same deal.
Put the idea of a **bigger flat** on hold and leave savings untouched.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a rumour on night shift that nobody will confirm.
Still able to **keep going**, but it stays at the back of his mind.
S1.quote: Precious in transport planning books every lorry out of the yard. If software does the booking, Precious is out before I am, and Precious has two kids.
fieldNote: He thinks first about **colleagues** with more to lose, especially Precious (the transport planner) with two kids.
Refuses AI tools out of **distrust** of data use, not fear of learning.
Sees the union as his **main lever**; individual plans come second.

steps.text: Ask the union rep to bargain a no-redundancy clause for new robots
Shelve the move to a bigger flat and leave savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, not promises. I'd be at every union meeting and probably at a demonstration outside the regional parliament, because if thinking AI runs the warehouse by 2028 and robots pick by 2031, that's every warehouse job in the region gone in five years. Online I'd be angry, and I wouldn't hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means I'm out of work at about thirty-two. The office goes first, so the people who plan our shifts and set our rates are software by 2028, and then the floor follows. And all those other warehouses nearby that make me feel safe now, they'd go the same way at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything big and get our savings up from a year to as close to two as I can. I'd push the union hard for long notice and proper redundancy pay, and I'd vote for whoever promises a basic income or a jobs guarantee. I'd probably look at something hands-on that needs a licence, maybe a gas fitter course, but I'd drag my feet, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'd be lying awake doing sums. Giulia's job is probably safer than mine, and part of me hates that I'd be leaning on her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Giulia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I've got two years, maybe three before the robots, and I don't have a plan. She'd say we'll be fine on her money, and I'd say that's not the point. I've paid my own way since I was sixteen, and leaning on my partner's nursing pay at thirty-two would kill me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at a gas fitter course but drag your feet. What stops you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hate starting over. I'm good at this job, I know every aisle, and going back to being the slow new guy at twenty-nine scares me more than I'd admit at the pub. And if robots do hands-on work by 2031 anyway, what's a gas course buying me, three years?

say: This is why workers need **laws, not promises**, and he'd join a **demonstration** to say so.
He'd warn that every warehouse job in the region could go in **five years**.
think: He expects to be **out of work** at about thirty-two, once robots arrive around 2031.
The **nearby warehouses** that feel like a safety net now would fall at the same time.
do: Stop **big spending** and push savings from one year towards **two years** of pay.
Press the union for **long notice** and proper redundancy pay.
Vote for candidates offering a **basic income** or jobs guarantee.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing sums about money.
**Ashamed** at the idea of leaning on his partner's nursing pay.
S2.quote: I've paid my own way since I was sixteen, and leaning on my partner's nursing pay at thirty-two would kill me.
fieldNote: The 2-year warning removes his **safety net** of plentiful local jobs, which shook him visibly.
Pride drives him: he hates **depending on his partner** more than the money itself.
Says he'd retrain but admits he'd **drag his feet**; the extra three years for robots feel too short to matter.

steps.text: Cut big purchases and raise savings towards two years of pay
Join union demonstrations for long notice and redundancy pay
Vote for parties promising a basic income or jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and no excuse. I'd want the union to start bargaining now, before AGI lands in 2031, for a fund that pays for retraining and early notice. I'd be loud about it, but less panicked than with the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years for the office and eight for us on the floor is enough time to do something, if I actually do it. That's the problem, I know I'd wait. But I'd be thirty-five when the robots come, and that's young enough to start something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for an evening course for a gas or electrical licence, the slow part-time one, so I'm not betting everything at once. I'd keep working and keep saving the 400 a month, maybe bump it to 500. And I'd stand for the union committee, which I've been avoiding for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of control. Like seeing the storm on the weather map days ahead. You still get wet, but you can at least find your coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last time you said you'd drag your feet. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. With two years I'd freeze. With five, I could sign up for a course without feeling like I'm drowning. I'd still be the guy who signs up in September and starts in January, but I'd start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the thinking parts of your job by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scanner already tells me where to go, so in a way the thinking part's already gone. What changes is the people above me: the shift managers and planners. If AI runs the rota and the pick rates, there's nobody human left in the warehouse to argue with, and that bothers me as a union man.

say: With **five years** of warning, there's **no excuse** for the union not to start bargaining now.
He'd want a **retraining fund** and early notice agreed before AGI lands in 2031.
think: Five years for the office and **eight for the floor** is enough time, if he actually acts.
At **thirty-five** when robots come, he'd still be young enough to start again.
do: Sign up for a **part-time evening course** towards a gas or electrical licence.
Raise monthly savings from **400 to 500** while still working shifts.
Stand for the **union committee** he has avoided for two years.
feel: **Anxious** but with some control, like a storm seen days ahead on the map.
S3.quote: If AI runs the rota and the pick rates, there's nobody human left in the warehouse to argue with, and that bothers me as a union man.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn **freezing into acting**; he'd start a course, slowly.
His sharpest worry is losing **human managers** to bargain with, not just his own job.
Knows he **procrastinates** and says so plainly.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time evening course for a gas or electrical licence
Stand for election to the union committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, so let's not waste it waiting for bosses to be kind. I'd push for laws that make companies share what they save from robots, maybe a tax that funds retraining. At the pub I'd say it calmly, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years for AGI and robots in 2039 means I'm about forty when the floor goes. That's a lot of my working life still left after that, which is the scary part. But it's enough time to get a trade properly, and Giulia and I could plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking for a few years and finish a full electrical apprenticeship part-time, even if it takes four years. I'd keep saving and maybe put some of it into a small flat to rent out, so there's income that isn't my body. And I'd campaign with the union for a robot tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, but slower. It's more like knowing the knee will go one day. You don't panic, but you don't forget it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be about forty when robots arrive. What does that mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forty's old for starting again but young for stopping. My uncle got laid off from the car plant at forty-three and never really worked again, just odd jobs. I don't want to be him, so I'd use the ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI tools. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd have to, for the electrical course, the books and quizzes are probably all on apps by then. I'd use it like a calculator, for the course, and that's it. I still wouldn't trust it with anything personal.

say: A decade is a **gift**, and nobody should waste it waiting for bosses to be kind.
He'd argue for a **robot tax** that pays for retraining.
think: With robots in 2039, he'd be **about forty** with much of his working life left.
Ten years is enough to **learn a trade properly** and plan with his partner.
do: Finish a full **electrical apprenticeship** part-time over about four years.
Put part of his savings into a **small rental flat** for income that isn't his body.
Campaign with the union for a **robot tax** to fund retraining.
feel: Still **anxious**, but slower, like knowing his knee will give out one day.
S4.quote: My uncle got laid off from the car plant at forty-three and never really worked again, just odd jobs.
fieldNote: His uncle's **layoff at forty-three** is the story he measures himself against.
With ten years he moves from protest to a **real plan**: a trade and a rental flat.
Would use AI only as a **calculator** for coursework, keeping his distrust.

steps.text: Complete a part-time electrical apprenticeship over four years
Buy a small flat to rent out with part of his savings
Campaign with the union for a robot tax funding retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. Every warehouse goes at once and there's nowhere to run, and I know I'd freeze. What would help is a law that says if a company brings in robots, workers get a year's notice, real retraining paid by the company, and a share of the savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cold, and you should. Everyone talks about robots, but right now people are getting chest infections in chilled every winter. If the robots are coming anyway, at least make the years we've got left decent.

headlineQuote: Forty's old for starting again but young for stopping.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old picker** in the chilled section of a grocery distribution centre, six years in.
He's a committed **union man**, with over a year's pay saved and a partner who nurses.
He calls AI **hype** in the calm world and turns to **collective bargaining** as change grows.
The **2-year AGI** picture leaves him alarmed; with more warning he'd retrain as an electrician, slowly.
He distrusts AI tools and admits he **drags his feet** on change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because every warehouse would go at once and he says he'd freeze.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving **a year's notice**, company-paid retraining and a share of savings when robots come in.
Decent conditions now, like **warmth** in the chilled section, for the years left.
